old: Riemann hypothesis (1859): the zeros of the zeta function, which control how evenly primes are spread, all lie on one line in the complex plane. Trillions of zeros have been checked, but no proof exists. A proof would sharpen countless results about primes.
new: Riemann hypothesis (1859): the nontrivial zeros of the zeta function, which control how evenly primes are spread, all lie on one line in the complex plane. Trillions of zeros have been checked. On 20 November 2026 Levent Alpöge of Anthropic posted a claimed proof of it, and of a stronger generalized version, made with Claude and written in Lean. Others have compiled the Lean code, but no human-readable proof exists yet and experts are still checking it (developing). Disclosure: this Lab is drafted with Claude. A proof would sharpen countless results about primes.
problem: Out of date: a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis was posted on 20 November 2026; also only the non-trivial zeros are meant.

old: P vs NP (1971): can every quickly checkable problem be quickly solved? (See computability.) Yang–Mills existence and mass gap: give a rigorous mathematical construction of the quantum theory behind the strong nuclear force and prove its lightest particle has positive mass. Hodge conjecture: certain topological features of algebraic shapes come from algebraic sub-shapes. Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer: the number of rational points on an elliptic curve is predicted by its L-function.
new: P vs NP (1971): can every quickly checkable problem be quickly solved? (See computability.) Yang–Mills existence and mass gap: give a rigorous mathematical construction of the quantum theory behind the strong nuclear force and prove its lightest particle has positive mass. In October 2026 OpenAI claimed an unreleased proof of the existence part only; it is unverified. Hodge conjecture: certain topological features of algebraic shapes come from algebraic sub-shapes. Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer: how many independent rational points an elliptic curve has (its rank) is predicted by its L-function at s = 1.
problem: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer was misstated (it predicts the rank, not “the number” of points); added OpenAI’s unverified Yang–Mills existence claim.

old: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (developing, November 2026): must smooth fluid flows in 3D stay smooth, or can they “blow up”? In September 2026 OpenAI announced an AI-generated, Lean-checked proof that the equations can blow up when a carefully designed smooth external force is applied, a case the Clay statement allows but many experts consider an artificial loophole. NYU’s Tristan Buckmaster, whose related work came first, disputes how OpenAI reached its method. On 20 November 2026 Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge posted a claimed AI-assisted proof of blow-up with no force at all, with some verification materials still to come. Neither claim has been independently verified, and Clay has not awarded a prize. Disclosure: this Lab’s text is drafted with Claude, made by Anthropic, where Alpöge works; the authors report using Claude.
new: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (developing, November 2026): must smooth fluid flows in 3D stay smooth, or can they “blow up”? On 8 September 2026 OpenAI announced an AI-generated, Lean-checked proof that they can blow up when a smooth external force is applied. Clay’s statement allows this case, but several experts see it as a side question, not the core problem. NYU’s Tristan Buckmaster, whose related work came first, disputes how OpenAI reached its method; OpenAI denies using his work. Clay said the problem “has apparently been settled” but is reviewing it slowly and has awarded no prize. On 20 November 2026 Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge posted a claimed AI-assisted, Lean-formalized proof of blow-up with no force, with some numerical data still to come; it is still being checked. Disclosure: this Lab’s text is drafted with Claude, made by Anthropic, where Alpöge works; the authors report using Claude and OpenAI’s Codex.
problem: One-sided and incomplete: experts disagree about the forcing; Clay said the problem has “apparently been settled”; OpenAI denies using Buckmaster’s work; the authors used Claude and Codex.

old: The simplest case is centuries old. Quadratic reciprocity (Gauss, 1796) links whether p is a square modulo q to whether q is a square modulo p. Langlands’ conjectures extend this kind of hidden harmony to all equations and all symmetry groups.
new: The simplest case is centuries old. Quadratic reciprocity, guessed by Euler and Legendre and first proved by Gauss in 1796, links whether an odd prime p is a square modulo another odd prime q to whether q is a square modulo p. Langlands’ conjectures extend this kind of hidden harmony to vastly more equations and symmetry groups.
problem: Quadratic reciprocity is for odd primes and was conjectured by Euler and Legendre before Gauss; “all equations and all symmetry groups” overstated.

old: Modularity, used to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem, is one case: the number of solutions of an elliptic curve modulo each prime matches the coefficients of a modular form. You can check one example yourself: the curve y² + y = x³ − x² and the form q ∏(1 − qⁿ)²(1 − q¹¹ⁿ)² agree prime by prime.
new: Modularity, used to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem, is one case: for an elliptic curve, the prime p minus the number of solutions modulo p equals the p-th coefficient of a modular form. You can check one example yourself with the curve y² + y = x³ − x² and the form q ∏(1 − qⁿ)²(1 − q¹¹ⁿ)². Modulo 5 the curve has 4 solutions, and 5 − 4 = 1, the coefficient of q⁵.
problem: Wrong rule: it is p minus the number of solutions that equals the coefficient, not the number of solutions itself.

old: Recent progress on old problems: In 2013 Yitang Zhang, then a little-known lecturer, proved there are infinitely many prime pairs less than 70 million apart; collaborative work (Polymath) and James Maynard cut the gap to 246. Also in 2013 Harald Helfgott proved the “weak” Goldbach conjecture for odd numbers. In 2019 Terence Tao proved that almost all Collatz sequences get close to small values.
new: Recent progress on old problems: In 2013 Yitang Zhang, then a little-known lecturer, proved there are infinitely many prime pairs less than 70 million apart; collaborative work (Polymath) and James Maynard cut the gap to 246 by 2014. In 2026 Julia Stadlmann lowered it to 240, then AI systems claimed 212 and then 186. Also in 2013 Harald Helfgott proved the “weak” Goldbach conjecture for odd numbers; it was computer-checked in 2026. In 2019 Terence Tao proved that almost all Collatz sequences get close to small values.
problem: Out of date: the prime-gap bound moved in 2026 (240 by Julia Stadlmann, then AI claims of 212 and 186); weak Goldbach was computer-checked.

old: Settled: Maryna Viazovska solved sphere packing in 8 dimensions in 2016 (and, with colleagues, in 24), earning a Fields Medal in 2022. In February 2025 Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture about how small a region can be while containing a needle pointing in every direction; Wang received a 2026 Fields Medal. Yu Deng, with Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma, rigorously derived the Boltzmann equation for gases from particle dynamics, progress on Hilbert’s sixth problem; Deng also received a 2026 Fields Medal.
new: Settled: Maryna Viazovska solved sphere packing in 8 dimensions in 2016 (and, with colleagues, in 24), earning a Fields Medal in 2022. In February 2025 Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture: a set holding a needle pointing in every direction can have zero volume, yet must still be fully three-dimensional. Wang received a 2026 Fields Medal. (OpenAI claimed an all-dimensions proof in October 2026; it is unverified.) Yu Deng, with Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma, rigorously derived the Boltzmann equation for gases from hard-sphere dynamics over long times, progress on Hilbert’s sixth problem; Deng also received a 2026 Fields Medal.
problem: Kakeya was described wrongly: such sets can have zero volume; the theorem is about dimension. Added an unverified 2026 all-dimensions claim and Deng’s long-time result.

new: In September 2026 OpenAI announced a claimed Navier–Stokes blow-up proof produced by many AI agents and checked in Lean (see the Millennium page). Many mathematicians think it is technically correct, but they raised concerns: whether the forced case meets the spirit of the problem, whether the Lean statements match the ordinary-language problem, how hard the AI-written proof is to understand, and credit for human researchers working on similar methods. new: Results are shared as preprints on arXiv (since 1991), then refereed by journals, which can take years. Errors are found after publication too. old: Conics turn up everywhere. Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. A parabolic dish sends every incoming ray to one point, which is how satellite dishes and solar cookers work. A ball thrown in the air follows a parabola.
new: Conics turn up everywhere. Planets move in ellipses, to a very good approximation, with the Sun at one focus. A parabolic dish sends every incoming ray parallel to its axis to one point, which is how satellite dishes and solar cookers work. A ball thrown in the air follows a parabola, if air resistance is ignored.
problem: Imprecise: a parabolic dish focuses rays parallel to its axis; thrown balls follow parabolas only without air resistance.

old: An infinite series converges if its partial sums settle on a number. ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … converges to 1. The harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … does not: it grows forever, though incredibly slowly. Tests such as the ratio test tell you which is which.
new: An infinite series converges if its partial sums settle on a number. ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … converges to 1. The harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … does not: it grows forever, though incredibly slowly. Tests tell you which is which: the ratio test settles the first, but for the harmonic series it gives no answer, and the integral test is needed.
problem: The ratio test gives no answer for the harmonic series; the integral test is needed.

old: A Taylor polynomial is built so its value, slope, curvature and higher derivatives all match the function at one point. Matching more derivatives makes it hug the curve over a wider range. Taylor’s theorem bounds the error, so you know how many terms you need.
new: A Taylor polynomial is built so its value, slope, curvature and higher derivatives all match the function at one point. For well-behaved functions, matching more derivatives makes it hug the curve over a wider range, though only within the series’ radius of convergence. Taylor’s theorem bounds the error, so you know how many terms you need.
problem: More terms help only inside the radius of convergence.

new: Riemann (1854) generalized this to spaces of any dimension, with a metric that says how to measure lengths at each point. Tensors are the bookkeeping tools for quantities like the metric and curvature, written so they do not depend on the choice of coordinates.

old: Proof assistants are now practical. The four colour theorem (2005), the Feit–Thompson theorem (2012) and the Kepler conjecture (2014) have been fully checked by computer. In 2020 Peter Scholze challenged the Lean community to check a difficult new theorem of his; they finished in 2022. Lean’s community library, mathlib, holds a large and growing share of undergraduate and graduate mathematics.
new: Proof assistants are now practical. The four colour theorem (2005), the Feit–Thompson theorem (2012) and the Kepler conjecture (2014) have been fully checked by computer. In 2020 Peter Scholze challenged the Lean community to check a difficult new theorem of his and Dustin Clausen; they finished in 2022. In 2026 AI agents began writing huge Lean proofs, including one of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
